content:
The SEO mistakes that hold back most Indian D2C stores are not exotic. They are built into the website: filter and sort URLs that create thousands of near-duplicate pages, category pages with no useful text, product pages that copy the manufacturer's description, slow mobile templates weighed down by apps and scripts, product markup that disagrees with the page, out-of-stock products deleted without a plan, and translated pages set up without the signals Google needs. Each of these is a build decision, which means it is cheapest to get right when the store is designed, and it is something any ecommerce website development partner in Pune should be able to check and fix on an existing store. This guide explains each mistake, how to spot it on your own site, and what the fix involves.

It is written for founders and marketing leads of D2C brands on Shopify, WooCommerce or custom platforms, especially those who have spent on ads for a year or two and want organic search to carry more of the load. We have kept it to problems we see repeatedly when auditing stores before a redesign, and we have avoided promising specific traffic gains: how much a fix helps depends on your category, competition and starting point, and anyone quoting a guaranteed percentage is guessing.

## How to check your own store first

You do not need paid tools to find most of these issues. Before reading on, open:

- **Google Search Console → Pages (indexing report).** Look at how many pages are indexed versus "Crawled – currently not indexed", "Duplicate without user-selected canonical" and "Alternate page with proper canonical tag". Large numbers of duplicates usually point to filter URLs or variant pages.
- **Search Console → Performance.** Filter by page to see whether category and product pages get impressions at all, or whether most traffic lands on the homepage and a few blog posts.
- **Search Console → Core Web Vitals** and **PageSpeed Insights** on one category page and one product page, tested on mobile.
- **Search Console → Enhancements / Shopping** sections for product markup errors and merchant listing issues.
- **A site: search** such as `site:yourstore.in` combined with a filter parameter you use, to see whether filter URLs are being indexed.

Keep these open as you go through the list.

## Mistake 1: Filters and sorting creating thousands of duplicate URLs

Most stores let shoppers filter by size, colour, price and brand, and sort by price or popularity. Each combination can produce a new URL: `/kurtas?colour=blue&size=m&sort=price-asc`. A catalogue of a few hundred products can generate tens of thousands of these. Search engines crawl them, find nearly the same products on each, and spend their crawling effort on pages that should never rank, while your real category and product pages are crawled less often.

Google published updated guidance on managing faceted navigation in late 2024, which describes the trade-off clearly: if you do not need filtered URLs to appear in search, prevent them from being crawled; if a small number of filtered views have real search demand (for example "black running shoes"), make those deliberate, crawlable pages with their own titles and content.

**What the fix usually involves:**

- Decide which filter combinations deserve to be landing pages (usually a small number with clear search demand) and build them as proper category or sub-category pages.
- Keep other filter and sort combinations out of the crawl, using approaches such as robots.txt rules for parameter patterns, or filters implemented so they do not create new crawlable links. Canonical tags pointing filtered views to the main category help consolidate signals but do not stop crawling.
- Keep URL parameters in a consistent order so the same filter set does not appear under several URLs.
- Make sure pagination works as normal links so products deep in a category can still be discovered.

We cover the options in detail, with Shopify and WooCommerce specifics, in our guide to [handling filters and faceted navigation without duplicate pages](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-faceted-navigation-seo-2026).

## Mistake 2: Category pages with nothing but a product grid

Category (or collection) pages are often the best pages on a store to rank for broad, high-intent searches: "cotton kurtas for women", "stainless steel water bottles", "organic jaggery powder". Yet many D2C stores leave them as a heading and a grid. Google has little to understand the page by beyond product names, and shoppers get no help choosing.

**The fix:** a short, useful introduction above the grid (two or three sentences on what the range includes and who it suits), clear sub-category links, and a section below the grid answering the real questions shoppers ask about the category: materials, sizing, how to choose, care. Write it for people. A paragraph stuffed with "buy cotton kurtas online India best price" helps nobody and falls under Google's keyword-stuffing guidance.

Also check that each category page has a unique title tag and meta description, and that you do not have two categories competing for the same search (for example "Kurtas" and "Kurta Sets" with almost identical products).

## Mistake 3: Copied or empty product descriptions

When a D2C brand also sells through marketplaces, or resells products, the same description often appears on many sites. Google tends to show one version of near-identical content, usually from a larger or older site. Other stores leave descriptions to one line, or paste the same templated paragraph across hundreds of products with only the name changed.

**The fix:**

- Write original descriptions for your bestsellers and highest-margin products first: who it is for, why choose it, a consistent specifications table, and the practical details people ask about (size, fit, care, what is in the box).
- Enter specifications as structured attributes or metafields, not prose, so they can also drive filters, schema and feeds.
- If you sell on marketplaces too, consider keeping the fullest, most detailed version on your own store.
- Use real customer questions, reviews and return reasons to decide what each description is missing.

AI tools can help draft from your product data, but every claim must be checked by someone who knows the product, and publishing large volumes of unreviewed generic text adds little and can fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy.

## Mistake 4: Slow mobile templates

Most Indian shoppers browse on phones, often on variable mobile connections. Google's Core Web Vitals measure loading (Largest Contentful Paint, with "good" at 2.5 seconds or less), responsiveness (Interaction to Next Paint, good at 200 milliseconds or less) and visual stability (Cumulative Layout Shift, good at 0.1 or less). Page experience is one of many ranking considerations rather than a dominant one, but a slow store loses shoppers regardless of rankings.

The usual causes on D2C stores:

- **Too many apps and plugins** each adding scripts: reviews, wishlists, pop-ups, chat widgets, upsell tools, multiple analytics and pixel tags.
- **Oversized images** uploaded straight from the camera or design tool, not resized or served in modern formats.
- **Heavy themes** with sliders, animations and features the store does not use.
- **Late-loading banners and pop-ups** that push content down and cause layout shift.
- **Slow hosting** on WooCommerce, or no caching and CDN.

**The fix:** audit every app and third-party script and remove what is not earning its keep; resize and compress images and serve WebP or AVIF; set explicit image dimensions; lazy-load images below the fold but not the main product image; and on WooCommerce, use proper hosting, caching and a CDN. Measure before and after with real-user data in Search Console, not just a single lab test. Our guide to [why Shopify and WooCommerce stores are slow and which fixes are worth paying for](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026) goes through each cause.

## Mistake 5: Product markup that disagrees with the page

Product structured data helps Google show price, availability and review information in search results, and feeds merchant listings. Problems we see:

- **Duplicate markup** from the theme and an SEO app both outputting Product schema, sometimes with different prices.
- **Stale prices or availability** in the markup when a sale ends or stock runs out.
- **Review markup for reviews that are not visible on the page,** or self-serving review markup on pages where Google does not support it.
- **Missing required properties** for merchant listings, such as price and currency.
- **Markup on category pages** describing a single product as though the category were one item.

**The fix:** output one consistent set of Product markup per product page, generated from the same data that renders the visible price and stock, and test with Google's Rich Results Test and the Search Console reports. Do not use markup to say anything the page does not show. The old version of this article suggested using structured data for GST; there is no such Google feature, and tax details belong on the invoice and checkout, not in search markup.

## Mistake 6: Deleting out-of-stock and discontinued products

D2C catalogues change constantly. When a product sells out or is discontinued, the quick reaction is to delete it, which turns a page with search history and backlinks into a 404, and lands shoppers from Google, old Instagram posts and WhatsApp forwards on an error page.

**The fix depends on the situation:**

- **Temporarily out of stock:** keep the page live, mark it out of stock (in the visible page and in the markup), offer a back-in-stock alert and show alternatives.
- **Permanently discontinued with a clear replacement:** redirect (301) to the replacement or the closest equivalent.
- **Discontinued with no replacement:** redirect to the most relevant category if that genuinely serves the visitor, or keep a page explaining the product is discontinued with links to alternatives. Returning a 404 or 410 is acceptable when there is truly no useful destination; redirecting everything to the homepage is not helpful.

Our guide to [what to do with out-of-stock, discontinued and deleted product pages](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-out-of-stock-discontinued-product-pages-seo-2026) covers the decision for each case.

## Mistake 7: Multilingual pages without the right signals

Some Pune and Maharashtra D2C brands add Marathi or Hindi versions of their store, which can be valuable for reaching customers who search in those languages. The mistakes are usually technical:

- Machine-translated pages published without review, which read poorly and convert badly.
- Language switched only by a script or cookie on the same URL, so search engines see one language.
- Missing or incorrect hreflang annotations, so Google cannot tell which page serves which language.
- Translated product pages with untranslated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text.

**The fix:** give each language its own URL (for example `/mr/` and `/hi/` folders), add reciprocal hreflang annotations including an x-default, translate titles and meta descriptions properly, load fonts that render Devanagari well without slowing the page, and start with the categories and products that matter most rather than translating everything at once. Do it only if you can support customers in that language after they buy.

## Mistakes that are not really SEO mistakes

A few things often blamed for poor rankings are better understood as business or measurement problems:

- **Judging SEO on traffic alone.** A store can gain traffic from blog posts that never sell anything. Measure organic revenue and conversions by landing page type in GA4.
- **Expecting quick results.** Structural fixes such as faceted navigation and category content often take weeks or months to show in rankings as Google recrawls the site.
- **Buying links.** Paid link packages risk a manual action and rarely help a store; genuine mentions, collaborations and good PR are slower but safer.
- **Changing everything at once.** If you redesign, re-platform, change URLs and rewrite content in the same week and traffic drops, you will not know why. Stage changes and keep a redirect map for any URL change.

## A practical order of work

If your store has several of these problems, an order that usually makes sense:

1. **Crawl and index control** (mistake 1): stops wasted crawling and duplicate pages.
2. **Speed** (mistake 4): helps every page and every shopper.
3. **Markup consistency** (mistake 5): quick to fix, prevents rich result problems.
4. **Out-of-stock handling** (mistake 6): set a rule so the problem stops growing.
5. **Category content** (mistake 2): highest value for broad searches.
6. **Product descriptions** (mistake 3): start with bestsellers, work outward.
7. **Multilingual** (mistake 7): only once the main language store is in good shape.

Record the date of each change so you can relate it to Search Console data later.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the most common SEO mistake on ecommerce sites?
Letting filter and sort options create large numbers of crawlable, near-duplicate URLs is one of the most common and damaging. It wastes crawling on pages that should not rank and dilutes signals across duplicates. Control which filtered views are crawlable and turn only the ones with real search demand into proper landing pages.

### Do category pages need text for SEO?
A short, useful introduction and a section answering common questions help both shoppers and search engines understand the page. Keep it genuinely helpful and avoid repeating keywords; a grid with no context gives Google little to work with for broad category searches.

### Should I delete out-of-stock products from my store?
Usually not. Keep temporarily unavailable products live and marked out of stock, with alternatives and a back-in-stock alert. For permanently discontinued products, redirect to a close replacement or relevant category where that genuinely helps the visitor.

### Does site speed affect ecommerce SEO?
Core Web Vitals are part of Google's page experience signals, which are one of many ranking considerations. Speed matters even more for conversions: slow mobile pages lose shoppers before they see the product. Audit apps, scripts and images first.

### How long does it take to see results from ecommerce SEO fixes?
It varies. Technical fixes such as markup corrections can show up within weeks as pages are recrawled, while structural changes and new category content can take several months to affect rankings. Track changes by date in Search Console to judge their effect.
